::: {.kw-overview}
This issue is dominated by efforts to widen and better-select the donor pool. A US registry analysis quantifies the tradeoff between accepting a higher-KDPI kidney now and waiting on dialysis for a better offer, while two cohorts probe the outer limits of living donation — five-year outcomes from donors aged 60 and older, and the prognostic weight of pre-donation donor albuminuria. On immunosuppression, a national OPTN/UNOS study links once-daily extended-release tacrolimus to modestly better graft survival than immediate-release formulations, and an Indian cohort ties higher tacrolimus exposure to BK polyomavirus reactivation, bridging the immunosuppression and infection threads. Cardiometabolic care features through a large Korean study showing that consistent time in the systolic blood-pressure target range tracks with better graft outcomes. Rounding out the issue, a meta-analysis weighs double-J against single-J ureteric stents, and a systematic review takes a sober look at AI and machine-learning models for predicting delayed graft function. Note: no full texts were available via PubMed Central for the selected papers in this run, so every summary below is grounded strictly in the PubMed abstract.
:::

---

### 1. [Survival Benefit Tradeoff: When a Lower KDPI Kidney Does Not Outweigh the Risks of Waiting](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0000000000005882)
[Masotti M, Lyden GR, Hart A, Miller JM, Schaffhausen CR. *Transplantation*, 2026. PMID: 42625262.]{.kw-ref}

Every deceased-donor offer forces a program and patient to weigh the quality of the kidney in front of them against the accumulating harm of more time on dialysis, and this analysis sets out to quantify that tradeoff explicitly. The authors used a modern period-prevalent cohort of adult, non-preemptive, kidney-alone candidates and recipients drawn from the US Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients, fitting Cox proportional-hazards models with time-varying coefficients modelled flexibly using splines. This let them characterise separately the rising mortality risk of longer waitlist dialysis exposure, post-transplant mortality, and the survival benefit associated with lower Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) offers, which was itself allowed to vary with time. From these they derived a novel measure — and a "tradeoff heat map" — expressing how many months on dialysis would offset the survival advantage of holding out for a lower-KDPI kidney, across values of KDPI, candidate age, and primary diagnosis. The headline conclusion is that for non-preemptive candidates each additional month of dialysis erodes the potential gains of waiting for a better offer, though the magnitude depends heavily on patient characteristics and on when in the waiting trajectory the offer arrives. The abstract reports the framework and direction of effect rather than specific hazard ratios, so the practical value lies in the decision aid rather than a single threshold. For UK practice, where organ offers are judged against the analogous Kidney Donor Risk Index, the work reinforces a more individualised, quantitative approach to offer acceptance — particularly counselling older or diabetic candidates that turning down a moderate-KDPI kidney to wait for a better one may cost more survival than it buys.

### 2. [Five-Year Patient and Graft Outcomes After Living Donor Kidney Transplantation From Donors Aged 60 Years and Older: A Single-Center Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.transproceed.2026.06.044)
[Thai KL, Truong HTT, Pham DM, Le PND, Hoang KC, Thai MS. *Transplant Proc*, 2026. PMID: 42624714.]{.kw-ref}

Recruiting older living donors is one way to expand the donor pool, but mid-term graft performance from these kidneys remains a live concern, which this single-centre retrospective cohort from Vietnam set out to address. The investigators studied 279 living-donor kidney transplants, grouping recipients by donor age into those from donors younger than 60 (n = 237) and those from donors aged 60 or older (n = 42), and applied inverse probability of treatment weighting to reduce selection bias. Outcomes were longitudinal recipient eGFR, patient survival, and death-censored graft survival over five years. Unadjusted five-year death-censored graft survival was lower with older donors (90.2% versus 98.2%; log-rank p = 0.0056), but after weighting this difference narrowed to 94.6% versus 98.3%, with a restricted mean survival time difference over 60 months of just −0.24 months (95% CI −1.02 to 0.24). Recipients of older-donor kidneys had modestly lower mid-term eGFR, generally by 4–7 mL/min/1.73 m², while five-year patient survival did not differ significantly. The authors conclude that carefully selected living donors aged 60 and over yield acceptable mid-term results and that donor age of 60 or more was not an independent predictor of graft loss, supporting expansion of living-donor criteria particularly in lower-resource settings. For UK programmes, which already accept many older living donors, this adds reassurance about mid-term graft survival while underlining that recipients should be counselled about somewhat lower baseline function — though the small older-donor subgroup and single-centre design temper the strength of the evidence.

### 3. [Association between donor albuminuria and the risk of graft failure in living-donor kidney transplantation: a retrospective cohort study](https://doi.org/10.1093/joneph/aajaf025)
[Yin S, Dong L, Li X, Lin T. *J Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42246577.]{.kw-ref}

As programmes accept more marginal living donors to ease organ shortages, the safety of donors with low-grade albuminuria has become a practical question this retrospective cohort tackles directly. The authors analysed 1,674 living donor–recipient pairs transplanted between 2017 and 2023, stratifying by pre-donation urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) into a high-uACR group (≥30 mg/g, n = 120) and a low-uACR group (<30 mg/g, n = 1,554) using KDIGO thresholds, with death-censored graft failure as the primary outcome assessed by Kaplan–Meier analysis and multivariable Cox models. Recipients of kidneys from high-uACR donors experienced substantially more death-censored graft failure than those from low-uACR donors (14.17% [17/120] versus 2.19% [34/1,554]; P < 0.001), and after full adjustment donor albuminuria carried a 2.13-fold increased risk (adjusted HR 2.13, 95% CI 1.02–4.46, P = 0.044). The hazard was markedly amplified when donors had both elevated uACR and hypertension or diabetes (HR 4.73, 95% CI 1.93–11.62, P = 0.001), and the association held across strata of donor pre-donation eGFR and in competing-risk and repeated-measurement sensitivity analyses. The authors judge uACR to have moderate predictive power and call for its incorporation into a broader donor risk-assessment framework rather than use as a sole gatekeeper. For UK living-donor assessment, where albuminuria is already part of donor workup, this quantifies the downstream graft risk and flags donors with combined albuminuria and cardiometabolic disease as a group warranting particular caution — noting the wide confidence interval and modest event numbers in the high-uACR arm.

### 4. [A Comparative Study of Once-Daily versus Twice-Daily Tacrolimus in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplant Recipients: A National Cohort Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.07.035)
[Gupta G, Gungor AB, Neyestanak ME, Hada MD, Azhar M, Ariyamuthu VK, Qannus AA, Pal V, Tanriover B. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42570723.]{.kw-ref}

Whether the once-daily extended-release tacrolimus formulation (LCP-tacrolimus, LCPT) offers any real-world graft-survival advantage over immediate-release tacrolimus has remained unsettled, and this national registry study provides the largest comparison to date. The authors conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of adult deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients in the OPTN/UNOS registry transplanted between 1 January 2018 and 30 June 2023 and discharged on tacrolimus plus mycophenolate, excluding multi-organ and living-donor transplants and anyone who switched formulation during the index admission. Exposure was the tacrolimus formulation at discharge — immediate-release brand, immediate-release generic, or LCPT — and the prespecified primary outcome was all-cause graft failure, analysed with inverse probability of treatment weighting-adjusted Cox models. Among 79,833 recipients, LCPT (n = 11,581) was associated with a lower adjusted hazard of all-cause graft failure than immediate-release brand tacrolimus (HR 0.877; 95% CI 0.797–0.965), whereas immediate-release generic and brand did not differ (HR 0.939; 95% CI 0.868–1.016). The signal held in a sensitivity analysis restricted to centres prescribing all three formulations (HR 0.872; 95% CI 0.789–0.963) and in a propensity-score-matched comparison of LCPT against combined immediate-release tacrolimus (HR 0.913; 95% CI 0.836–0.998). The authors frame this as a modest but consistent adjusted reduction in graft-failure risk with the extended-release formulation. For UK units, where immediate-release tacrolimus predominates on cost grounds, this observational signal argues for a closer look at once-daily formulations, while the potential for residual confounding by indication and the absence of randomisation counsel caution before changing practice.

### 5. [Unlocking the impact of BK virus in renal transplant recipients in North India: viral load dynamics, genotypes, and clinical outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trim.2026.102449)
[Padhy S, Dey S, Bora I, Sarkar S, Sharma A, Sethi J, Sharma V, Mohi GK, Ratho RK, Nada R. *Transpl Immunol*, 2026. PMID: 42624173.]{.kw-ref}

BK polyomavirus reactivation can progress to graft-damaging nephropathy, and this exploratory study links its emergence to the intensity of tacrolimus exposure in a North Indian transplant population. The investigators screened 90 kidney transplant recipients for plasma BK viral DNA by real-time PCR, with clinical follow-up and tacrolimus trough data available for 57; recent exposure was estimated as the mean trough over the six months preceding testing (Tac C₀–6m), intrapatient variability as the coefficient of variation, and genotyping was performed on three representative positive samples. BK viral DNA was detected in 13 of 90 recipients (14.4%), and those who were positive had significantly higher recent tacrolimus exposure than negative recipients (median Tac C₀–6m 7.38 versus 5.30 ng/mL; P = 0.002). Mean recent trough concentration also correlated positively with plasma viral load (Spearman's ρ = 0.588, P = 0.035), whereas neither time from transplantation to positivity nor tacrolimus variability reached significance. No significant differences emerged between positive and negative recipients in acute rejection, calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity, decoy cells, or transplant-related death. The authors read this as support for individualised immunosuppression and routine BK surveillance, since higher cumulative tacrolimus exposure appears to track with reactivation. For UK practice, where quantitative BK PCR monitoring and pre-emptive immunosuppression reduction are already standard, the study reinforces the rationale for that approach, though its small, single-centre, exploratory design and limited genotyping mean it is hypothesis-generating rather than practice-defining.

### 6. [Association Between Systolic Blood Pressure Time in Target Range and Graft Outcomes in Kidney Transplant Recipients: Result From KOTRY and KNOW-KT](https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.125.048247)
[Koh HB, Kim HJ, Park CH, Ryu JH, Jung HY, Kim MG, Han S, Kang KP, Lee KW, Park JB, Kang SH, Ban TH, Huh KH, Kim MS, Kim BS, Yang J. *J Am Heart Assoc*, 2026. PMID: 42622144.]{.kw-ref}

Single blood-pressure readings capture a moment rather than the consistency of control, and this study tests whether the proportion of time a recipient's systolic pressure stays within target better predicts graft fate. Using two Korean cohorts — the nationwide KOTRY registry as the main cohort (4,559 recipients) and the multicentre KNOW-KT study for replication (828 recipients) — the authors calculated systolic blood-pressure time in target range (SBP-TTR) within 110 to 130 mm Hg by linear interpolation of office readings at 6, 12, and 24 months after transplantation. The primary outcome was a composite of death-censored graft loss or a 50% or greater decline in eGFR, over a median follow-up of four years. Each 1-standard-deviation increase in SBP-TTR was associated with a 20% lower risk of the composite outcome (adjusted HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.71–0.91), and compared with recipients who spent no time in range, those in the 1–50%, 51–99%, and 100% bands had progressively lower risks (adjusted HRs 0.69, 0.63, and 0.47 respectively). The associations were stronger among recipients of deceased-donor kidneys, older or female donors, and those with higher baseline systolic pressure, were reproduced in the replication cohort, and did not extend to all-cause death after adjustment (adjusted HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.71–1.09). The authors conclude that sustained systolic control within 110–130 mm Hg may matter for graft preservation while calling for randomised trials to confirm causality. For UK transplant follow-up, it strengthens the case for consistent, not merely occasional, blood-pressure control and suggests time-in-range as a monitoring metric worth considering.

### 7. [Double-J versus single-J stent placement in kidney transplant recipients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postoperative outcomes](https://doi.org/10.4285/ctr.25.0096)
[Shenelo SA, Julianto SA. *Clin Transplant Res*, 2026. PMID: 42618454.]{.kw-ref}

Ureteric stents reduce urological complications after kidney transplantation, but whether the double-J or single-J design performs better remains contested, which this systematic review and meta-analysis set out to resolve. The authors searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, EBSCO, Wiley, and Springer through 10 April 2025 for randomised and observational studies comparing the two stent types, extracted data following PRISMA guidance, and assessed risk of bias with the Cochrane tool and the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, analysing six studies covering 3,479 patients in RevMan. Double-J stents were associated with a lower risk of urinary tract infection than single-J stents (OR 0.58; 95% CI 0.46–0.73; P < 0.0001), lower serum creatinine at six months (mean difference −8.15 µmol/L; 95% CI −12.08 to −4.22; P < 0.0001), and shorter hospital stay (mean difference −5.62 days; 95% CI −5.79 to −5.45; P < 0.0001). Against these benefits, double-J stents carried a more than threefold higher risk of ureteral stenosis (OR 3.42; 95% CI 1.47–7.99), while delayed graft function, urine leakage, haematuria, and eGFR did not differ significantly between the designs. The authors conclude that double-J stents reduce infection, shorten admission, and improve early creatinine but at the cost of increased stenosis risk. For UK surgeons, this offers a structured basis for stent selection and counselling on the infection-versus-stricture trade-off, though the small number of pooled studies, mixed study designs, and an implausibly tight hospital-stay confidence interval suggest the estimates should be read cautiously.

### 8. [Prediction of delayed graft function after kidney transplantation using artificial intelligence and machine learning: A Systematic Review](https://doi.org/10.1159/uin/aewag012)
[Yadav S, Yadav A, Bais SS, Khurana U, Sharma A, Jha P. *Urol Int*, 2026. PMID: 42623334.]{.kw-ref}

Delayed graft function is a common early complication, and this PROSPERO-registered systematic review appraises how well artificial-intelligence and machine-learning models built on routine clinical variables actually predict it. Following PRISMA guidance, the authors searched MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library without date restriction for studies developing or validating AI/ML models for delayed graft function from routine donor, recipient, immunological, laboratory, ischaemia-time, and perioperative variables, appraising quality with PROBAST+AI and STREAM-URO. Of 613 records, 12 studies were included, most of them retrospective deceased-donor cohorts with three drawing on national registries, and reported delayed graft function incidence varied widely from 12.5% to 56.8%. The models spanned neural networks, logistic and penalised regression, support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting, and stacked ensembles, with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve ranging from 0.67 to 0.99; recurrent predictors included donor renal-function measures, donor age and body mass index, donation after circulatory death, ischaemia time, recipient body size, dialysis exposure, and HLA matching. Crucially, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and external validation were uncommon, and PROBAST+AI rated eight of the twelve studies at high overall risk of bias. The authors conclude that these models show promise but that their incremental benefit over conventional regression is inconsistent and that heterogeneity, limited transparency, and scant external validation must be addressed before routine use. For UK teams weighing algorithmic decision-support, the review is a useful caution against adopting delayed-graft-function prediction tools before they are externally validated and shown to be clinically useful.
